title: Attention Signal / Call-and-Response ("Give Me Five", "Class-Yes")
description: A short, taught signal — a clap-in or snap-in, a call-and-response phrase, or "Give Me Five" — that brings the whole room back to shared attention without the teacher raising their voice. Because the signal is rehearsed, students know exactly what to do (voices off, eyes on the board), which keeps the room calm and preserves a positive classroom culture. Edutopia frames these as tools so that "raising your voice" is never the only option.
whenToUse: Reach for it whenever the room is loud, students are "engaged in a loud activity," or attention has drifted and you need to give directions — especially after partner or small-group work. Use the same signal every time so it becomes automatic. Edutopia presents these as useful for middle and high school teachers.
howTo:
1. Choose one signal you can use consistently.
2. Explicitly teach the expected response ("voices are off, eyes are on the board").
3. Demonstrate and rehearse — for older students this "will likely take only a few minutes."
4. Deliver at normal volume and wait for 100%.
5. Reuse the identical signal all year; add a quieter version (snaps) for a higher quiet standard.
example: In 10th-grade biology, partner talk about a lab prediction has gotten loud. Instead of talking over it, the teacher raises a hand and says "Give me five"; students finish their sentence, put pencils down, and turn toward the board. Within about five seconds the room is quiet and she gives the next direction in a normal voice.
videoTitle: Teacher Toolkit: Attention Signal (Secondary)
sourceName: Edutopia — "7 Attention-Getters to Use Instead of Raising Your Voice"

title: Countdown Transition Routine
description: A spoken countdown that gives students a clear, predictable window to finish, pack, move, and be ready — treating the transition as a taught procedure with a clear beginning and end. Edutopia describes announcing seconds remaining and slowly counting down from five; Responsive Classroom adds that pacing must be taught, named, modeled, and practiced — transitions "happen with kids, not to them."
whenToUse: Use it at every predictable hand-off: stopping work, cleaning up, moving into groups or back to seats, packing up. It's the right move when a transition drags and instructional time leaks — Edutopia notes saving 15 minutes a day yields "45 extra hours of instructional time per year." Give it as an advance warning, not only after chaos starts.
howTo:
1. Name the transition and the finished state.
2. Give an advance warning so students can reach a stopping place.
3. Count down aloud at a steady pace and narrate progress.
4. Start the next activity exactly at zero.
5. If the class misses the standard, re-teach and rehearse rather than lecture.
example: An 8th-grade English teacher ends station work: "You have 30 seconds to return materials and be seated — counting down from five." She narrates ("Table three is set, Marcus has his book open") and hits "one" as the last student sits, then starts the debrief immediately so the countdown means something.
videoTitle: Classroom management: The Countdown
sourceName: Edutopia — "Mastering Classroom Transitions" (with Responsive Classroom, "Teaching Transitions")

title: Timed Transitions with a Visual or Audio Cue
description: A visible or audible timer that makes remaining time concrete so students pace themselves and the change of activity feels predictable. Texas SPED Support defines a Visual Countdown as "a teacher-controlled transition support that provides students with a flexible, visual representation of time remaining," used to "support transitions between activities by providing a structured cue" and to "promote independence." Edutopia suggests a stopwatch and publicly announced seconds remaining.
whenToUse: Use for timed work blocks and the final minutes of an absorbing activity, since a predictable end "reduce[s] resistance by offering a predictable end to preferred activities." It also stretches engagement in non-preferred tasks by "gradually extending participation." Pair with a verbal cue: "In 5, we will clean up."
howTo:
1. Project a timer or set up a removable visual countdown all students can see.
2. Introduce with a verbal cue ("In 5, we will clean up").
3. Remove markers / let time run "at appropriate intervals."
4. At zero, complete the transition immediately.
5. Use the same tool daily so the cue, not your voice, carries the message.
example: A high-school geometry teacher projects a five-minute timer for a warm-up: "When the timer chimes, pencils down and we compare answers." At one minute: "In one, we go to the board." Students wrap up on their own and the chime ends the task.
videoTitle: Smooth Transitions: The Key to Classroom Efficiency
sourceName: Texas SPED Support (TEA) — "Visual Countdown"

title: Entry/Exit Routine (Do Now / Bell Work)
description: A consistent, taught sequence for the first and last minutes of class: enter, assigned seat, materials out, start meaningful work on the board unprompted, then a clear pack-up procedure. Conscious Teaching's secondary materials give a four-step routine (assigned seat, materials out, bag under chair, begin bell work) and stress: "make sure you start class on time with meaningful work" — "a concrete, teachable way to get them to a particular point in the class without nagging."
whenToUse: Use at the start of every period so the opening minutes belong to learning, and mirror it at the end (a "Pack and Stack"-style close, per SUNY Geneseo). Especially valuable in secondary rooms where students arrive from a passing period and you need the opening for attendance. Re-teach — including how to enter when late — whenever entry slips.
howTo:
1. Define 3–5 observable entry steps and post them.
2. Put a short, content-based Do Now on the board daily, completed silently ("10 Minutes Maximum").
3. Teach and rehearse the routine, including late entry and how not to do it.
4. Circulate and reinforce students who reach the final step.
5. Mirror it with a fixed exit procedure.
example: In a Wewoka 9th-grade U.S. History class, three bell-ringer questions are projected before the bell. Students sit in assigned seats, stow bags, and write while the teacher takes attendance and greets latecomers quietly at the door. Four minutes in: "Level 4 in here today," and she moves into reviewing answers.
videoTitle: Teach Like a Champion Technique 28 - Entry Routine
sourceName: Conscious Teaching — "Start of Class Procedures" (secondary)

title: Clear Expectations & Posted Classroom Norms
description: Stating, posting, and teaching the small set of behaviors and procedures that make the room run. The IRIS Center distinguishes norms ("familiar ways of interacting in a classroom"), expectations ("desired behaviors or outcomes"), rules ("written expectations for behavior"), and procedures ("patterns for accomplishing classroom tasks"), and describes an effective classroom as one that "runs smoothly, with minimal confusion and down time" and "maximizes student learning."
whenToUse: Establish and teach in the first days of the year/semester; re-teach after breaks or when routines drift. Return to them whenever you see repeated confusion or "down time" around a procedure — a sign the expectation wasn't observable enough. Use them as the reference point before any correction.
howTo:
1. Name the few expectations that matter, written as observable, positively stated behaviors.
2. Convert each into procedures for specific routines.
3. Post and teach explicitly with examples and non-examples.
4. Support consistently — acknowledge expected behavior, correct by referring to the norm.
5. Reevaluate periodically and revise what isn't working.
example: A Wewoka algebra teacher and her classes turn three school-wide expectations into a posted chart: what "respectful, responsible, ready" look and sound like during notes, partner work, and quizzes. When a student calls out, she taps the chart — "Notes voice — raise a hand" — and moves on. In October the class revises the group-work row.
videoTitle: Classroom Expectations That Stick: Co-Creating Agreements With High School Students | Episode 14
sourceName: IRIS Center (Vanderbilt) — "Establishing Classroom Norms and Expectations"

title: Consistent Consequences System / Behavior Matrix
description: A classroom matrix turning school-wide expectations into observable behaviors per routine, paired with an in-class continuum of acknowledgements and consequences so responses are predictable, not personal. The PBIS California TAC high-school handout describes Tier I classroom procedures as expectations, routines, acknowledgements, and "an in-class continuum of consequences," built by asking "What would you see and hear?" Entries must be observable, measurable, positively stated ("I tell students what TO do"), understandable, and always applicable.
whenToUse: Build it at the start of the year with students and use it every time you acknowledge or correct, so students get the same response day to day. Lean on it for high-friction secondary routines: entering, using an agenda, turning in and tracking assignments. Decide in advance what you handle in class vs. refer out, and keep interactions at "4:1 positive to negative teacher statements."
howTo:
1. List your classroom routines.
2. With students, define observable, positively stated behaviors for each.
3. Attach the continuum: acknowledge → prompt → re-teach → error correction → in-class consequence, with clear referral criteria.
4. Teach the matrix and move through acquisition, fluency, maintenance, generalization, adaptation.
5. Self-monitor consistency and praise ratio; re-teach rather than escalate when a whole class slips.
example: A Wewoka team posts a one-page matrix for entry, notes, group work, and exit with a four-step in-class response ladder. When a student keeps talking during notes, the teacher uses the same sequence she always uses — nonverbal cue, quiet private reminder, brief in-class consequence — and the student knows what comes next. Because the hallway shares the matrix, students stop testing individual teachers.
videoTitle: MPS PBIS Classroom Matrix
sourceName: PBIS California TAC — "The Power of the High School Classroom Matrix"

title: Proximity Control
description: Moving near a student as a quiet reminder of the expectation, without stopping the lesson. The IRIS Center defines it as "a strategy in which the teacher reduces the physical distance between herself and a student as a way to remind that student of behavioral expectations," standing "within three feet" for "a few seconds" while continuing to teach. It is part of active supervision, can "increase student engagement and reduce problem behaviors," and has "no associated costs."
whenToUse: Use while teaching or monitoring whole-group, small-group, independent, and seatwork — scan for engagement and early off-task signs, then move. It's the right first move for "minor, non-dangerous behaviors." Use it proactively by circulating in "unpredictable patterns" so your presence supports everyone rather than singling one student out.
howTo:
1. Arrange the room so you can reach every student.
2. Scan continuously while teaching.
3. Move within about three feet, keeping instruction going without comment.
4. Stay only a few seconds — "avoid lingering for long periods of time."
5. Walk away, keep circulating, "circle back if necessary."
example: During an 11th-grade chemistry lecture, two students start scrolling phones. Without breaking her sentence, the teacher walks down that row and stands near their bench a few seconds; phones go away. She keeps moving and passes again two minutes later — no one else notices anything happened.
videoTitle: Proximity Control: High School Example & Non-Example
sourceName: IRIS Center (Vanderbilt) — Fundamental Skill Sheet: "Proximity Control"

title: Non-Verbal Redirection Cues (hand signal, eye contact, gesture)
description: A small set of taught silent cues — gesture, look, hands-up, printed sign — that redirect off-task behavior or affirm on-task behavior without pulling the class off track. Houston ISD states they "redirect undesirable classroom behavior or affirm positive student behavior" via "facial expressions," "gestures," "body posture," and "position," "redirecting students without diverting the attention of the entire class." Reading Rockets calls silent signals "an effective way to foster communication while limiting interruptions during instruction."
whenToUse: Use for low-level, frequent behaviors during instruction — side talk, phone out, head down — when stopping the lesson costs more than the behavior. Use a hands-up cue when you need "the class' attention immediately." Reserve distinct individual cues for students who "need distinct cues," and build cues only for the behaviors that matter most.
howTo:
1. Identify the behaviors most often needing correction or encouragement.
2. Choose cues that are "simple," "discrete," and "relevant to the classroom rules."
3. Tell students why cues will be used, then "introduce and model the cues one at a time."
4. Teach the expected response and give practice.
5. "Implement cues immediately and consistently"; add a silent thumbs-up on compliance.
example: Mid-lesson in 7th-grade math, a student pulls out a phone. The teacher makes eye contact, taps her own pocket (the taught "phone away" cue), and keeps explaining; the phone disappears. Thirty seconds later she catches his eye and gives a thumbs-up. The lesson never pauses.
videoTitle: Non Verbal Cues: Keep Students on Task Without Saying a Word
sourceName: Houston ISD Effective Practices — "Non-Verbal Interventions"

title: Strategic Seating Chart
description: Deliberately deciding who sits where, and in what configuration, so the room quietly supports focus. Edutopia reports seating shapes "who they talk to," "how well they focus," and "how they engage with a lesson," is "some of the most powerful tools that teachers have to manage a classroom," and works "quietly behind the scenes to promote prosocial behavior and suppress distractions." A SUNY Geneseo teaching text is blunter: "letting students sit where they want to is an invitation to disaster!"
whenToUse: Assign seats from day one and match configuration to the activity: rows to limit distraction during lectures and independent practice; clusters for brainstorming, peer review, collaboration; horseshoe for whole-class discussion. Change seats when an arrangement isn't working — "at least once a quarter," or the same day if a plan fails. Use it proactively for students who need to be near the front, near you, or away from a specific peer.
howTo:
1. Build the chart before students arrive; assign every seat.
2. Leave clear paths so you can reach the whole room.
3. Place students by attentiveness, focus/executive-function needs, and peer combinations.
4. Match desk configuration to the day's activity rather than one static layout.
5. Revisit on a schedule and adjust immediately when a placement fails.
example: For a new semester of 10th-grade English, the teacher uses rows for a modeling/writing-heavy unit, splitting two students who feed off each other and seating a student with hearing needs up front. For literature circles she moves to clusters of four, mixing talkative and quiet students. When one cluster becomes a social hub, she moves two students the next day.
videoTitle: Student Seating Chart Best Practices: The Most Under Utilized Tool for Classroom Management
sourceName: Edutopia — "Research-Based Tips for Optimal Seating Arrangements"

title: Positive Narration / Behavior-Specific Praise
description: Naming out loud the exact behavior a student or group is doing well, so expectations get reinforced by what you notice. The IRIS Center defines behavior-specific praise as "a positive statement directed toward a student or group of students that acknowledges a desired behavior in specific, observable, and measurable terms," where the teacher "explicitly states the exact behavior the student demonstrated." It can "increase positive behavior and decrease challenging behaviors" and beats general praise like "Good job!"
whenToUse: Use during instructional time, transitions, and down time — scan for students already doing the expected thing and name it "immediately following a desired behavior." When one student is off task, praising a nearby peer pulls the class back without embarrassing anyone. Keep the ratio high: "four praise statements for every one reprimand," about "six praise statements every 15 minutes," applied equitably.
howTo:
1. Teach the expectation, then look for students meeting it.
2. Name the student and the exact behavior ("Johanna, thank you for cleaning up immediately when I rang the science bell").
3. Deliver immediately, no lecture attached.
4. Tally to hold a 4:1 ratio; increase frequency (every few minutes) for students who struggle to stay engaged.
5. Make it age-appropriate — middle/high schoolers "may prefer subtle praise statements," so go quiet, private, or written when public praise would stigmatize.
example: Two minutes into partner work in 9th-grade biology, the teacher circulates and narrates: "Table two already has the hypothesis written. Dani, thanks for getting your partner started." An off-task student picks up his pencil unprompted. Later she drops a quiet aside to a self-conscious student — "Solid annotation on paragraph three" — instead of praising him publicly.
videoTitle: Behavior-Specific Praise: Secondary Example & Non-Example During Small-Group Discussion
sourceName: IRIS Center (Vanderbilt) — "Page 2: Behavior-Specific Praise"

title: 2x10 Relationship-Building
description: A short, deliberate investment in one relationship: two minutes a day, ten school days in a row, of non-academic conversation with the same student. West Virginia PBIS defines it as educators who "select a student and for 2 minutes a day, 10 days in a row… engage in a brief conversation with that same student," emphasizing brevity, student voice ("students are invited to share something non-academic with a caring adult"), and honesty. Critically, "the content of your conversation should not relate to the student's schoolwork or behavior."
whenToUse: Choose a student you've struggled to connect with, who is struggling, who is "habitually quiet," or who doesn't participate. Greater Good in Education says use it any time but "especially at the beginning of the year," and lists it as appropriate for middle and high school. Build the two minutes into existing moments — before school, passing time, lunch, seat work, hallways, after school.
howTo:
1. Pick one student.
2. Find a natural two-minute window and protect it for ten consecutive school days.
3. Talk about anything non-academic and share something about yourself too.
4. Keep schoolwork and behavior entirely off the table.
5. After ten days, keep connecting informally.
example: A Wewoka teacher picks a junior who has been shutting down. For two weeks she catches him two minutes as he walks in — his truck project, hunting season, a band he likes — never mentioning missing work. By week two he warms up in class, and when she does redirect him, he takes it from her.
videoTitle: 2x10 Strategy
sourceName: West Virginia PBIS — "2x10 Relationship Building"

title: Positive Greetings at the Door
description: Greeting each student individually at the door so class starts with connection, a reminder of expectations, and immediate work. The Center on PBIS calls it "an effective strategy for increasing academic engagement, decreasing unwanted behavior, and improving student-teacher relationships." Research materials describe a multi-component strategy pairing an authentic individual greeting with pre-corrective reminders, a high-interest entry activity, and a brief private repair conversation when needed, creating "behavioral momentum for behavioral engagement."
whenToUse: Use it daily as students transition in from less structured settings like the hallway or PE, because problem behavior "before instruction begins" can "set a negative tone for the remainder of the class period." Be at the door before students start entering. Use it deliberately with any student who struggled last period or yesterday — that's the moment for a private restorative word.
howTo:
1. Stand at or near the door before the passing period ends.
2. Greet each student individually and authentically, by name, in a developmentally and culturally appropriate way.
3. Add a brief pre-corrective reminder for the first activity.
4. Have a high-interest entry activity ready.
5. For any student you had a negative interaction with, hold a brief, private restorative conversation at the door.
example: A Wewoka teacher greets each student by name before third period — "Morning, Kayla, warm-up's on the board." As a student who blew up yesterday walks in, she says quietly, "Glad you're here. Yesterday's done — let's have a good one." He nods and sits. By the bell most of the class is already writing.
videoTitle: Greetings at the Door for Middle & High School | Let's Learn GA!
sourceName: Center on PBIS — "Practice Briefs: Positive Greetings at the Door"

title: Least-Invasive Intervention
description: A scaled toolkit for correcting off-task behavior with the smallest possible footprint. Teach Like a Champion: "The best teachers keep instruction center stage and maintain strong relationships with students by correcting nonproductive behavior consistently and with finesse," keeping "the thread of instruction intact," maximizing "students' privacy," and maintaining "emotional constancy." The handout lists nonverbal intervention (visual/voice), positive group correction, anonymous individual correction, private individual correction, lightning-quick public correction, and consequence — explicitly "not sequential steps."
whenToUse: Use the moment behavior turns nonproductive and "threaten[s] to derail a lesson" — pick the least intrusive tool that will work rather than defaulting to a public callout. Favor the private end whenever you can preserve "as much student privacy as possible," escalating only if the smaller move doesn't land. Prevention first: "Prevention Beats Cure."
howTo:
1. Scan constantly so you catch behavior early.
2. Start nonverbal — look, gesture, vocal shift — while you keep teaching.
3. Step up to a positive group correction or anonymous individual correction that names the behavior, not the student.
4. Move to a private individual correction (whisper at the desk) when the issue needs naming.
5. Only then a lightning-quick public correction or in-class consequence — always with emotional constancy and a stated solution.
example: Two students in 10th-grade world history start talking during independent reading. The teacher first catches one student's eye and glances at the text; when talk continues she tells the room, "Check yourself — silent reading, eyes on the page." When one keeps going she walks over and whispers, "Page 214, start there," then steps away. The class never stops reading.
videoTitle: Least Invasive Intervention | Teaching Unpacked with Doug Lemov
sourceName: Teach Like a Champion (Uncommon Schools) — "Least Invasive Intervention"

title: Private / Non-Public Correction ("silent redirection")
description: A brief, quiet, respectful correction delivered to one student, so they get clear information without an audience. Understood describes respectful redirection as "a quick, in-the-moment strategy to give corrective feedback to students" that gets attention "without making a big deal about it," using a calm tone, neutral body language, and few words telling students "exactly what they're doing incorrectly" and "what they should be doing instead." In PBIS schools it may be called "error correction"; Teach Like a Champion's equivalent advice is to "Use a Whisper to Upgrade."
whenToUse: Use in the moment when a student is off task and the behavior interferes with their learning or others'. First ask "What is this behavior communicating?" — some students look off task while using strategies (standing, fidgeting) that keep them engaged. Prefer it over public correction with secondary students, where being called out in front of peers most often triggers defensiveness.
howTo:
1. Make sure the expectation was taught with examples and non-examples.
2. Decide in the moment whether the behavior is genuinely interfering.
3. Move close and correct quietly — calm tone, neutral body language, few words, name the behavior and the replacement.
4. Give a moment to comply and step away rather than standing over them.
5. Reinforce once they follow the redirection.
example: Mid-lesson in 8th-grade science, a student has his head down with a blank lab sheet. The teacher crouches beside his desk: "Head up, start with question one — I'll check back in two minutes," then walks away. Two minutes later, two answers are written and she says softly, "That's what I'm looking for." No one else was pulled into it.
videoTitle: How to redirect students without embarrassing them
sourceName: Understood.org — "Respectful redirection: A behavior strategy for teachers"

title: De-escalation Script and Calm Body Language
description: A prepared, calm way of responding when a student is dysregulated so your body and words lower the temperature. Edutopia explains that under perceived threat the "thinking parts" of students' brains go offline and the prefrontal cortex — "the rational decision-making part of the brain" — shuts down, so the teacher responds "in a calm and predictable manner that models the behavior we hope students will learn." The Crisis Prevention Institute adds concrete moves: be empathetic and non-judgmental, use empathic listening, stand "between 1-3 feet away," and allow time for decisions.
whenToUse: Use when a student becomes upset or is in distress — shutting down, taking neutral feedback "in a more hostile, exaggerated way," refusing to participate, or melting down over a small obstacle. Use it instead of a normal correction, which they can't process in that state. Know limits: most teachers "are not trained to be, nor should they be expected to act as, mental health professionals or crisis counselors" — bring in administration or counselors.
howTo:
1. Regulate yourself first — slow speech, lower volume, neutral face and posture.
2. Respect personal space: 1–3 feet, off to the side, explaining your actions if you must move closer.
3. Listen empathically — undivided attention, eye contact, nodding — and restate their words without judging the feelings.
4. Use a short consistent script, offer a limited choice, then allow time to think.
5. Hand off to admin/counseling when needed, and reconnect privately afterward.
example: A junior slams his laptop after a low quiz score and mutters he's "too dumb for this class." The teacher steps to the side of his desk, about two feet away, drops her voice: "That grade isn't the whole story. You can take two minutes at the back table or step to the hall with me — your choice," then waits without repeating herself. He takes the back table; she checks in ten minutes later.
videoTitle: 15 De-Escalation Strategies for the Classroom (Avoid Power Struggles & Stay Calm)
sourceName: Edutopia — "5 Strategies to Deescalate Behavior When Students Are Dysregulated"

title: Active Supervision (Move, Scan, Interact)
description: A deliberate monitoring routine defined as "the process of monitoring learning and performance on classroom expectations and rules that incorporates moving, scanning and interacting with students." Missouri SW-PBS describes three components — moving effectively, scanning effectively, interacting frequently — that "verbally and non-verbally, communicates to students the certainty that you do inspect what you expect." Research cited there says it "may reduce incidents of minor problem behavior while increasing appropriate behavior" and "may lead to increases in student engagement."
whenToUse: Use it any time students are working — independent practice, labs, group work — because "when supervising work or activities, circulate among students." Build it into lesson design by planning groupings, location, and activity level so you can reach every part of the room. Lean on it where minor off-task behavior usually starts, since there is "a relationship between the number of supervisor-to-student interactions and the instances of problem behavior."
howTo:
1. Plan groupings, materials, and layout so you can reach every student.
2. Move continuously and unpredictably, moving close to targeted areas.
3. Scan by sweeping all areas regularly, making brief eye contact with distant students, looking and listening for early signs of a problem.
4. Interact frequently — show interest, assist with tasks, give feedback.
5. Pair scanning with positive contacts so supervision feels like attention, not surveillance.
example: During independent practice in 11th-grade algebra, the teacher loops the back row, cuts across the middle, and pauses at three tables. Every 20 seconds she sweeps the room and catches a student in the far corner who hasn't started, reaching him with "Start with number one — I'll be back," and keeps moving.
videoTitle: Active Supervision: Secondary Example and Non-Example
sourceName: Missouri SW-PBS — Teacher Tool: "Classroom Active Supervision"

title: Strategic Circulation (Circulate)
description: Planned movement rather than random wandering: Teach Like a Champion defines Circulate as "the act of moving strategically around the classroom to build relationships with students and to maximize engagement and achievement," noting "a great teacher leverages her proximity and moves strategically." The purpose is to "move systematically and engage students while teaching" and to "gather data via observation, provide feedback, and make sure students are engaged in rigorous work during independent work time."
whenToUse: Use it during independent and partner work when you need live data on who understands the task, and while teaching so proximity spreads across the whole room. Plan your route in advance so no corner becomes a blind spot. Make it your default posture whenever students are producing work you could read over their shoulders.
howTo:
1. Plan a route that reaches every seat; ensure furniture leaves full physical access.
2. Move systematically while teaching, not just during work time.
3. Read student work as you pass and gather data on who is stuck.
4. Give short, specific feedback in passing and keep moving.
5. Use what you collected to reteach to the whole class or return to specific students.
example: In 9th-grade English during a timed paragraph, the teacher walks a planned loop, whispers "topic sentence first" to one student, and notices four students missing the same transition. She stops the class for 30 seconds, models it, and resumes her loop.
videoTitle: Circulation: Classroom management skill
sourceName: Teach Like a Champion (Uncommon Schools) — "Circulate"

title: Classroom Calm Corner / Reset Space
description: A small, defined area inside the classroom "set up to help students take a break, calm emotions, and reset," where students "remain in the classroom" under teacher supervision. Hennepin County's secondary guide notes "all students can benefit from calming resources when emotions are running high," listing benefits including self-regulation, keeping behavior from escalating, and minimizing lost learning time. Edutopia adds that framed positively, students "develop essential self-regulation skills" and "normalize managing emotions in a healthy way."
whenToUse: Teach it before anyone needs it so students learn the tools "before they need them," and be explicit about when it applies (anxious, angry, sad, overwhelmed) and when it does not ("to avoid taking a test," "to avoid presenting a group project"). Point students toward it early, at first signs of escalation. Expect students to "come back to work as soon as they are able."
howTo:
1. Find an area "a little bit away from the main area" — even "a bin on the floor in the corner" works.
2. Engage students in designing the space and setting expectations as a class agreement.
3. Stock it with a defined seat, posted guidelines, fidgets, calming images, a timer, and a reflection form.
4. Explicitly teach the calming techniques — deep breathing, journaling, seated stretches.
5. Establish a check-out and return process so students self-monitor their time.
example: A Wewoka teacher sets up a two-seat "Reset Table" behind a bookshelf with a timer, breathing card, stress ball, and reflection slip; students wrote the three posted rules. When a junior's jaw tightens after a text, she nods toward the table; he takes four minutes and is back before the period ends.
videoTitle: How to Use Calm Corners (So They Actually Help)
sourceName: Hennepin County Public Health — "Creating Calm Spaces in Schools: Secondary" (with Edutopia)

title: Class Pass Break Request
description: A structured way for a student to request a short, legitimate break instead of escaping work through disruption. PENT calls the Class Pass Intervention "a research-based intervention" letting students "appropriately request brief breaks from non-preferred academic tasks by exchanging earned 'Class Passes'" and also bank them "for rewards and privileges." Research indicates it is "highly effective at reducing behavior problems and increasing academic engagement," and "the time allowed for breaks is easily made up by the increased academic engagement time."
whenToUse: Use it with a student whose behavior functions to "avoid or escape doing academic work" seen as "difficult," "boring," or "otherwise 'aversive'." Prompt the pass "at the earliest signs of disruptive behavior," before escalation. Pair it with academic support so the student moves from spending passes to banking them.
howTo:
1. Identify a break location and short alternate activity (5–10 minutes).
2. Set break length — research supports "a 5-minute break for secondary-level students."
3. Decide rewards so "the more passes mean the better the reward."
4. Teach it with Tell, Show, Do, Feedback.
5. Give about "3 passes per" class period, prompt use at first signs, and offer the choice to take a break or bank the pass.
example: A Wewoka sophomore who melts down at the start of writing tasks gets three laminated passes each English period. When he pushes the paper away, the teacher asks, "Pass or push through?" He takes five minutes, returns, finishes the paragraph — and later starts saving passes for a Friday homework exemption.
videoTitle: SBIS: Structured Breaks and Class Pass
sourceName: PENT (California Positive Environments Network of Trainers) — "Class Pass"

title: Community-Building Circle
description: A structured circle conversation where every voice gets equal space, used proactively for "building the relationships and skills students need to support one another." Edutopia notes circles help students process "their thoughts and feelings" so they can "be more present in class," and warns "you can't 'restore' a community that you haven't built or sustained." IIRP adds that the circle implies "community," "connection," "inclusion," "fairness," "equality," and with "neither head nor tail" establishes "a level playing field for all participants."
whenToUse: Run circles regularly before problems appear, since they work best as "an integral part of school culture." Use one after "a particularly stressful class or noisy hallway experience," or when a sensitive issue is on students' minds. Alert support staff when a topic may need follow-up, and state the limits of confidentiality first.
howTo:
1. Build the relationships, skills, and shared values a circle depends on.
2. Establish circle practices: honor the talking piece, listen, you may pass, "speak and listen from the heart," "what is shared in circle, stays in circle."
3. State confidentiality limits — threats of harm must be reported.
4. Seat everyone in an actual circle and pass the talking piece in a sequential go-around.
5. Use circles for varied purposes and keep them scheduled.
example: Every Friday a Wewoka U.S. History teacher circles the desks for 12 minutes and passes a smooth stone. One week the prompt is light; the week after a hallway fight it is "what does it feel like in this building right now." Students may pass, and by November even the quietest take the stone.
videoTitle: Restorative Justice in Oakland Schools: Tier One. Community Building Circle
sourceName: Edutopia — "Building Community With Restorative Circles" (with IIRP, "Circles")

title: Restorative Conversation with Affective Questions
description: A short, scripted one-to-one conversation after a conflict that focuses on the incident, not the student's character. NSW Education describes restorative conversations as structured discussions that "address incidents of conflict or harm," "promote a positive approach to resolving conflict," and "stabilize the identity of all students involved," using questions that "elicit empathy, remorse and learning." IIRP notes "Why did you do that?" is "absent from the list" because it is "not helpful or relevant."
whenToUse: Use it after a conflict, disruption, or harm between students — in "one-to-one conversations," "small groups," or "more formal restorative mediation conferences." It is also the right move for re-entry after a removal. Recognize "in some situations there are no 'quick fixes'."
howTo:
1. Set up a private, calm conversation and start empathetically.
2. Ask "What happened?" and listen to understand, focusing on timeline not blame.
3. Validate feelings and needs — "I can see you are feeling frustrated"; "What did you want?" — avoiding interrogation and judgment.
4. Move to impact: "Who has been affected by what happened? In what way?"
5. Close on repair: "What do you need to do to make things right?" and "What would you do differently?"
example: Two 10th graders trade insults and one storms out. At passing period the teacher meets each for three minutes with the restorative questions. One offers an apology; the other agrees to ask for a seat change next time. Both return the next day without a referral.
videoTitle: How to Use the Restorative Questions in Student Discipline
sourceName: NSW Department of Education — "Affective questioning" (with IIRP "Restorative Practices Continuum")

title: Classroom Ticket / Token Recognition System
description: A visible acknowledgement system where students earn tokens for demonstrating posted expectations and exchange them for rewards. PENT describes a token economy as a visual support that "is a permanent reminder of the identified classroom rules," "provides concrete feedback on demonstration of desired behavior(s)," and "allows a student to see and understand when they will access reinforcement." PBIS Apps stresses "the ticket is really a reminder" for adults, and that the practice most associated with fewer referrals and more equitable discipline was that expected behaviors "were acknowledged regularly."
whenToUse: Use it when you want expectations reinforced continuously, and when acknowledgements have drifted toward the same few students. Give tokens frequently at first, then thin the schedule as behavior becomes routine. Always pair the ticket with a spoken, behavior-specific reason.
howTo:
1. Identify target behaviors and display them beside the token board.
2. Choose your token and a visual that shows progress.
3. Teach that tokens have value and can be exchanged at a designated time.
4. Deliver frequently when new, then reduce frequency.
5. Audit equity — list five students easy to praise and five who aren't, and spread acknowledgement "naturally, equitably, and for all students."
example: A Wewoka science teacher keeps tickets in her lab coat. When a student cleans a station unasked or restates a classmate's idea, she hands over a ticket and names the behavior. Tickets go in a jar for a Friday drawing, and twice a week she checks that they aren't all going to the same four students.
videoTitle: Teacher Toolkit: Tickets Reward System (High School)
sourceName: PENT — "Token Economies" (with PBIS Apps ticket-systems article)

title: Team-Based Group Contingency (Good Behavior Game)
description: A team goal for behavior with a shared reward that turns peer influence toward the expectations. Minnesota DOE defines a group contingency as one that "uses group reinforcement to capitalizes on peer influence" — "If a GROUP MEETS GOAL FOR BEHAVIOR then that GROUP OF STUDENTS IS REWARDED" — with the purpose "to prevent behavioral problems and increase appropriate behaviors." CEC calls group contingencies "an evidence-based, proactive classroom behavior management system" that rewards teams "contingent on following explicitly stated behavioral expectations."
whenToUse: Use it during the stretch of class that gets loose — long independent work, clean-up, the last fifteen minutes — for a defined window, not all period. Choose the type deliberately: interdependent applies "positive peer influence," independent minimizes peer pressure, dependent lets one student earn the reward for everyone. Watch for "students sabotaging or blaming peers."
howTo:
1. Pick target behaviors and state them positively, tied to posted expectations.
2. Choose contingency type; ensure any targeted student "is capable of the target behavior."
3. Set and post the goal and criterion in advance.
4. Announce start and stop, and track marks visibly and neutrally while circulating.
5. Deliver rewards promptly to every team that met the goal — more than one team can win.
example: For the last 20 minutes of a Wewoka geometry block, the teacher announces "Game on," splits the class into three balanced teams, and posts two target behaviors with a three-mark allowance. Two teams win and start homework early with music; the third gets a clean slate next game.
videoTitle: Good Behavior Game Animated Modeling Video for Teachers
sourceName: Minnesota Department of Education — "Group Contingencies Tip Sheet" (with CEC teacher's guide)

title: Cell Phone Parking Lot (Phone Storage Routine)
description: A taught, numbered storage routine that gives every phone a home for the period, protecting attention without daily negotiation. Edutopia cites research from May and Elder that "media multitasking interferes with attention and working memory, negatively affecting GPA, test performance, recall, reading comprehension, note-taking, self-regulation, and efficiency," and Jonathan Haidt: "Even when students don't check their phones, the mere presence of a phone damages their ability to think." The goal is an environment that encourages "flow — that optimal and focused experience."
whenToUse: Launch it on day one of a semester, and use it when asking students to keep phones in backpacks or face-down has already failed. Secure administrator support and inform families first so the routine is backed up when tested. Expect initial resistance — many students later report feeling "much more focused in class."
howTo:
1. Talk with your principal and confirm they'll back you up.
2. Notify parents and guardians before starting.
3. Get a wall holder with numbered slots and assign each student a number alphabetically in a shared spreadsheet.
4. Post one copy of assignments by the holder, keep a second at your desk.
5. Build drop-off into your entry routine and hold yourself to the same standard.
example: A shoe-organizer with 32 numbered pockets hangs by the door; students park phones on the way in right before bell work and collect them on the way out. The teacher's own phone goes in slot zero. After a rocky first week it takes eight seconds a student, and she stops policing screens.
videoTitle: Teacher Toolkit: Cell Phone Parking Lot (High School)
sourceName: Edutopia — "A Cell Phone Policy That Works in High School Classrooms"

title: Positive Phone Call Home
description: A short call to a family sharing something specific and good a student did, made "before there is a negative reason to call, such as bad grades, missing work, or a behavior issue." ASCD reports parents are often surprised by a positive call — even parents of well-behaved students — and students return to class with "a smile," "a thank-you," and appreciation "that someone noticed them for something other than a mistake," building relationships based on "respect, acknowledgment, and appreciation."
whenToUse: Call right away when a student shows creativity, compassion, courage, a success, or a kindness toward a classmate. Front-load it in the first week by calling at least one parent a day or making several calls on chosen days. Prioritize students colleagues have warned you about and students who arrive withdrawn or cautious.
howTo:
1. Note one specific thing the student said or did that day.
2. Call, identify yourself, and ask whether it's a bad time.
3. Say up front you're calling about something the student said or did — "Hi. This is Mr. Mali. I hope I haven't called at a bad time, I just wanted to talk to you about something your son said today."
4. Describe the specific action concretely, not in general praise.
5. Thank the family, and tell the student the next day that you called.
example: A Wewoka teacher notices a quiet junior helping a classmate through a lab procedure unasked. That afternoon she calls his mother, who answers warily, and opens with "He's fine — I'm calling because of something good he did today." The student walks in taller next class, and his mom emails twice that semester about college applications.
videoTitle: Making Positive Phone Calls Home
sourceName: ASCD / Educational Leadership — "Good Reasons to Call Home"

title: Ask Three Before Me
description: A short, taught routine that reroutes routine student questions through three peer/self-check sources before they reach the teacher. Students check their own work or notes, ask a nearby classmate, and check a posted resource (anchor chart, board, directions) — and only then raise a hand for the teacher. Because the three checks are rehearsed and posted, the room stays productive during independent work and the teacher can circulate instead of standing at a hand-raise queue. It also doubles as a live formative-assessment signal: when three peers on a table can't answer the same question, the whole class likely needs a reteach.
whenToUse: Reach for it during independent practice, seat work, station rotations, or group tasks — any time you keep getting the same procedural questions ("What page?", "Do we skip this one?", "How do I start?"). Not during silent quizzes, direct instruction, or when a student is in genuine distress; teach students the exceptions explicitly.
howTo: Introduce, model, rehearse, then reinforce. (1) Name the three checks students must do before the teacher: self/notes → nearby peer → posted resource or directions. Post them on the wall. (2) Model it out loud: raise your own hand, narrate walking through the three checks, then ask the teacher. (3) Practice with a low-stakes task in the first weeks so it becomes automatic. (4) When students ask you a procedural question, respond first with "Did you ask three before me?" and defer to peers; consistency early is what makes it stick. (5) Listen for questions that come back after three peers — those are your reteach signals, not a discipline problem. (6) State exceptions clearly (quiet work, quizzes, direct teaching, safety).
example: Second grader in Ms. Coleman's room raises a hand mid-independent-reading. The teacher points to the "Ask 3 Before Me" chart. The student checks the directions, asks the two students at the table ("I think you skip the blue one"), and then goes back to work. When the question comes back a fourth time from a different table, Ms. Coleman calls the class together for a 60-second reteach of the direction rather than answering it individually six times.
videoTitle: 60-Second Strategy: Ask 3 Before Me
sourceName: Edutopia (60-Second Strategy)
